reasons: The checks are detailed, but I did not run them, so I cannot confirm they pass.
A green run can include skipped checks when npx is not installed, so skips should be read as unverified.

terms.meaning: Running one test many times, once for each entry.
Asking pytest to find tests without running them, to confirm the names are valid.
The TypeScript compiler, which checks frontend code without producing output.
A command that runs a tool installed for a Node project.
The runner's check that tells whether a mutation is already present in a file.
A separate program started by this test to run a tool.

sections.name: File setup
sections.title: Setup and purpose
sections.what: Explains that the checks run in the ordinary suite, then loads the registry and the runner module.
sections.why: The top description says the checks run quickly so a broken entry is found before the slow mutation run.
sections.watch_out: Loading the runner at the top means an error in the runner stops this whole file from running.

sections.name: ids
sections.title: Entry names for labels
sections.what: Produces the list of entry names used to label each check.
sections.why: Gives each generated test a readable name that points at its entry.

sections.name: TestEveryEntryStillApplies (part 1)
sections.title: Anchor and Python parse checks
sections.what: Checks that each target file exists, that each find text appears exactly once, that the change alters the text, and that Python entries still parse after the change.
sections.why: A missing or duplicated anchor makes an entry meaningless, and a syntax error would fail tests for the wrong reason.
sections.watch_out: The parse check covers Python only, so frontend entries are checked by the compiler instead.

sections.name: TestEveryEntryStillApplies: test_a_frontend_mutation_still_typechecks
sections.title: Frontend compile and target checks
sections.what: Writes each frontend entry into its real file, runs the TypeScript compiler, and restores the file. It then checks that frontend test paths exist and that each entry names at least one test.
sections.why: A mutation that fails to compile would look like a kill, and a test path that does not exist would also look like a kill.
sections.watch_out: The check writes into a tracked source file during the run, so an interruption before the restore would leave the file changed.

sections.name: TestEveryEntryStillApplies: test_every_named_test_can_be_collected
sections.title: Collection, equivalence and reason checks
sections.what: Asks pytest to collect every named test in one run, requires each equivalence note to be substantial and give a reason, and requires each reason note to be longer than a short phrase.
sections.why: A wrong test name would fake a kill, and an unexplained equivalence would hide a real gap.
sections.watch_out: The equivalence check looks for a few keywords, so a note could pass by using one of them without giving a real proof.

sections.name: TestTheRegistryCoversWhatItShould
sections.title: Registry coverage and budget condition
sections.what: Checks that names are unique, that entries reach both top-level folders and several packages, that equivalent entries are at most one in five, that the answered-objection equivalence still holds, and that the known past defects remain in the registry.
sections.why: Stops the registry from covering only one area and looking complete, and guards against past defects coming back.
sections.watch_out: The budget check reads the pipeline's tier table, so raising any tier to three passes makes its equivalence note wrong.

sections.name: TestEveryReplacementIsDistinctive
sections.title: Replacement text must be unique
sections.what: Checks that each replacement text does not already exist in its target file.
sections.why: The runner uses the replacement to tell a moved anchor from a committed mutation, so a common replacement would cause false alarms.
sections.watch_out: Replacements that look like ordinary code need a marker comment to stay unique.

sections.name: TestTheHaltDetectorFitsEveryEntry
sections.title: Halt detector checks
sections.what: Checks that the runner's halt detector does not flag an unmutated file, does flag a mutated file, and reports a moved anchor as broken rather than as a committed mutation.
sections.why: A wrong detector would either stop a clean run or let a committed mutation pass unnoticed.
sections.watch_out: These checks call a private helper in the runner, so renaming it breaks them.

summary: Checks that every entry in the mutation registry still points at real code and real tests, so a refactor that breaks an entry fails here within seconds.
purpose: Keeps the registry honest. It stops an entry from silently matching nothing, matching twice, or naming a test that does not exist.
why: Without these checks, a moved mechanism would make the runner report the tests as inadequate, when the real problem is the entry.
how: For each entry, the checks confirm the file exists, the find text appears once, the change alters the text, Python still parses, frontend changes still compile, named tests can be collected, equivalence notes carry reasons, and the replacement is not already present. Other checks confirm coverage across packages and that the halt detector behaves correctly.
inputs: The MUTATIONS list, the source files it names, and the frontend project for the compiler check.
outputs: Pass, fail or skip results within the ordinary test suite.
risks: The frontend check briefly writes a mutated version into a real source file and restores it in a finally block. An interruption that skips the restore would leave the source changed. The frontend check and the collection check both depend on external tools, and a missing tool shows as a skip.
debug: Read the parametrized test name, since it is the entry name. An occurrence count failure means the anchor has moved or been duplicated in that file. A compiler failure means the mutation breaks the TypeScript build; run the compiler in the frontend folder to see the message. A skip means a tool was missing, so the check did not run.
